Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 107, verses 1–7:

This small surah, consisting of only seven verses, and those verses short ones, contains a great truth. On studying it, one feels that it virtually transforms the symbols of Islam, and on reflection a person sees the meaning of faith (iman) and disbelief (kufr) changing completely. Beyond this, the surah tells us what the temperament of the Islamic worldview (nazariya-e-hayat) is, and how great a good and benefit for humanity lies hidden within it. And from this it also becomes known how great a mercy Allah has shown to humanity by sending His final mission to it.

The truth is that this religion is not merely a name for some outward rituals, acts of worship and religious symbols. In it, religious aims, symbols and acts of worship are not beneficial unless they are sincere and their performance is solely for the pleasure of Allah. And when they do not produce in the human heart such effects as impel a person to righteous deeds, and unless these effects take on a form of conduct through which human life is reformed for the Hereafter, and in this world too they do not bring about reform and progress.

Furthermore, this religion is not a faith divided into scattered parts and fragments, such that a person may take whichever part he wishes and leave whichever part he wishes. It is a complete system of life and a way of living (minhaj-e-hayat). Its rites of servitude and its symbols are interconnected; its individual obligations and collective commandments are bound together and mutually supportive. The purpose of all its parts is one, and they relate to humanity: that humanity be granted purification of heart and soul, that their lives be made good, that people be mutual helpers, sponsors of one another, and step together on the path of goodness, progress and reform. And that their lives become a model of Allah's mercies.

A person says with his tongue that he is a Muslim; he is a Muslim, and accepts all the commands and decisions of the religion of Islam; he offers prayer, and performs other rites of servitude besides prayer. Yet despite this, the reality of faith and the confirmation of religion and faith are far removed from him. This is because the reality of faith has certain signs, and these signs show that the reality of faith exists. When these signs are absent, how can anyone say that the reality of faith exists? If there are no signs, there is only mere verbal profession of faith and a few outward rites of servitude.

The truth is that when the reality of faith fully settles in a heart, it immediately appears in the form of righteous deeds, as we have explained in detail in Surah al-'Asr. If a person's faith is not animated in this manner, the outward sign would be that faith does not in fact exist at all. This is the great truth which this surah presents in the form of a complete resolution.

*Ara'aytal-ladhi ... al-miskin* (107:1–3): "Have you seen the one who denies the recompense? That is the one who drives away the orphan, and does not urge the feeding of the needy." The beginning is with a question so that all turn their attention to it, in order to gain knowledge about such a person: who is he who denies the religion? And the Qur'an itself is explicit that such a person is a denier of the religion. Accordingly the answer comes.

*Fa-dhalika alladhi ... al-miskin* (107:2–3): "That is the one who drives away the orphan, and does not urge the feeding of the needy."

In view of the traditional definition of faith and religion, this explicit statement of the Qur'an may appear strange at first sight, but it is the real truth that one who drives away the orphan is in fact denying the religion. To drive away the orphan means to harm him and to humiliate him. And *wa-la yahuddu* (107:3) means that he does not urge other people to this act and does not take care of the needy. If he had accepted Islam with sincerity, and had true confirmation in his heart, he would not drive away the orphan, and he would urge and move people to feed the needy.

The truth is that the acknowledgment and confirmation of religion is not merely a divine act, but a mental and inner revolution, as a result of which a person automatically begins to show mercy and goodness to humanity, to those who deserve assistance and favours. Allah's demand is not that people merely recite a few words with their tongues. Alongside these words, Allah's demand is also for deeds which confirm that faith exists; otherwise faith would be merely a floating particle that drifts here and there in the air.

In these three verses, the way this truth has been stated with such clarity is not matched anywhere in the whole Qur'an, because it is the spirit of the Islamic worldview and the temperament of this religion.

We do not wish to enter here into the juristic definitions of Islam and faith and the debates and differences concerning their limits and conditions. Such definitions are made so that legal rights and obligations may be decided upon them. What is said in this surah expresses the reality as it is (haqiqat-e-nafs al-amri), which is valid before Allah and is measured by Allah's standard. The realities before Allah are different from those according to which legal matters are settled in the Shari'ah and in law. After this, according to this reality and principle, certain practical forms are mentioned:

*Fa-wayl lil-musallin ... al-ma'un* (107:4–7): "So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make a show of it, and withhold small kindnesses." This is a curse or a threat against those who are heedless of their prayer. Who are they? Those who make a show, and who do not give even the small necessities to others.

These people do pray, but they do not establish the prayer; it is not within the prayer. Their souls are estranged from the reality of prayer. Their thoughts are far from the meanings of what they recite. The recitation, supplications and praises that they read, their souls are far from them; it is as though they are heedless of the very prayer they are performing. They do not perform it properly. What Allah desires is that prayer be established correctly; mere performance is not what is required, and prayer is established only when it is recited with its religious spirit and its meanings, and in which the presence of Allah's Being is kept in mind.

For this reason, the prayer that they are performing does not produce its effects in their lives, because they are heedless during the movements of prayer. Accordingly, these people do not even give the small necessity (ma'un) to others. They do not perform any assistance, kindness or goodness to others, whereas the demand of prayer is that the worshipper does good to Allah's servants and does not withhold small necessities from them. Therefore those of this kind are in fact not performing true prayer. Hence, the standard of true and genuine worship before Allah is that a person does not withhold small necessities from humanity, and does not withdraw from helping them.

Thus we find ourselves confronted with another inseparable truth of the religion, and it is the demand of the Islamic worldview: a Qur'anic verse openly threatens worshippers that they will face destruction, because they are not establishing prayer properly. Rather, they are performing movements that have no spirit in them. They are not present in the court of Allah during these movements. They are not sincerely for Allah; rather, they pray merely to be seen by people, so the effects that true prayer produces do not appear from their prayer, neither does prayer affect their hearts, nor does it influence their practical world. Therefore this prayer is worthless as a particle, a mere dust, and for the worshipper it is rather a calamity and destruction.

After these explanations, it becomes clearly understood why Allah sends messengers to people and why it is demanded of people that they believe and serve. This entire striving brings no benefit to Allah; He is the Self-Sufficient King. The purpose is that human lives themselves be made good, their welfare is intended, their hearts be purified and their lives be successful. He desires for them a life founded upon pure consciousness and lofty ideals, within which people are sponsors of one another, whose mentality is noble, within which there is love and brotherhood, and whose outlook and conduct are both pure.

Alas! Where is humanity heading, having abandoned this goodness? Where is it wandering, having abandoned this mercy? And into what depths has it fallen, having abandoned this beautiful, graceful and lofty station? Or where is it lost in the intricate and dark paths of ignorance (jahiliyyah), while before it the light, the light of Islam, stands present at the central crossroads.

On studying it, one feels that it virtually transforms the symbols of Islam, and on reflection a person sees the meaning of faith (iman) and disbelief (kufr) changing completely. Beyond this, the surah tells us what the temperament of the Islamic worldview (nazariya-e-hayat) is, and how great a good and benefit for humanity lies hidden within it. And from this it also becomes known how great a mercy Allah has shown to humanity by sending His final mission to it.

The truth is that this religion is not merely a name for some outward rituals, acts of worship and religious symbols. In it, religious aims, symbols and acts of worship are not beneficial unless they are sincere and their performance is solely for the pleasure of Allah. And when they do not produce in the human heart such effects as impel a person to righteous deeds, and unless these effects take on a form of conduct through which human life is reformed for the Hereafter, and in this world too they do not bring about reform and progress.

Furthermore, this religion is not a faith divided into scattered parts and fragments, such that a person may take whichever part he wishes and leave whichever part he wishes. It is a complete system of life and a way of living (minhaj-e-hayat). Its rites of servitude and its symbols are interconnected; its individual obligations and collective commandments are bound together and mutually supportive. The purpose of all its parts is one, and they relate to humanity: that humanity be granted purification of heart and soul, that their lives be made good, that people be mutual helpers, sponsors of one another, and step together on the path of goodness, progress and reform. And that their lives become a model of Allah's mercies.

A person says with his tongue that he is a Muslim; he is a Muslim, and accepts all the commands and decisions of the religion of Islam; he offers prayer, and performs other rites of servitude besides prayer. Yet despite this, the reality of faith and the confirmation of religion and faith are far removed from him. This is because the reality of faith has certain signs, and these signs show that the reality of faith exists. When these signs are absent, how can anyone say that the reality of faith exists? If there are no signs, there is only mere verbal profession of faith and a few outward rites of servitude.

The truth is that when the reality of faith fully settles in a heart, it immediately appears in the form of righteous deeds, as we have explained in detail in Surah al-'Asr. If a person's faith is not animated in this manner, the outward sign would be that faith does not in fact exist at all. This is the great truth which this surah presents in the form of a complete resolution.

*Ara'aytal-ladhi ... al-miskin* (107:1–3): "Have you seen the one who denies the recompense? That is the one who drives away the orphan, and does not urge the feeding of the needy." The beginning is with a question so that all turn their attention to it, in order to gain knowledge about such a person: who is he who denies the religion? And the Qur'an itself is explicit that such a person is a denier of the religion. Accordingly the answer comes.

*Fa-dhalika alladhi ... al-miskin* (107:2–3): "That is the one who drives away the orphan, and does not urge the feeding of the needy."

In view of the traditional definition of faith and religion, this explicit statement of the Qur'an may appear strange at first sight, but it is the real truth that one who drives away the orphan is in fact denying the religion. To drive away the orphan means to harm him and to humiliate him. And *wa-la yahuddu* (107:3) means that he does not urge other people to this act and does not take care of the needy. If he had accepted Islam with sincerity, and had true confirmation in his heart, he would not drive away the orphan, and he would urge and move people to feed the needy.

The truth is that the acknowledgment and confirmation of religion is not merely a divine act, but a mental and inner revolution, as a result of which a person automatically begins to show mercy and goodness to humanity, to those who deserve assistance and favours. Allah's demand is not that people merely recite a few words with their tongues. Alongside these words, Allah's demand is also for deeds which confirm that faith exists; otherwise faith would be merely a floating particle that drifts here and there in the air.

In these three verses, the way this truth has been stated with such clarity is not matched anywhere in the whole Qur'an, because it is the spirit of the Islamic worldview and the temperament of this religion.

We do not wish to enter here into the juristic definitions of Islam and faith and the debates and differences concerning their limits and conditions. Such definitions are made so that legal rights and obligations may be decided upon them. What is said in this surah expresses the reality as it is (haqiqat-e-nafs al-amri), which is valid before Allah and is measured by Allah's standard. The realities before Allah are different from those according to which legal matters are settled in the Shari'ah and in law. After this, according to this reality and principle, certain practical forms are mentioned:

*Fa-wayl lil-musallin ... al-ma'un* (107:4–7): "So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make a show of it, and withhold small kindnesses." This is a curse or a threat against those who are heedless of their prayer. Who are they? Those who make a show, and who do not give even the small necessities to others.

These people do pray, but they do not establish the prayer; it is not within the prayer. Their souls are estranged from the reality of prayer. Their thoughts are far from the meanings of what they recite. The recitation, supplications and praises that they read, their souls are far from them; it is as though they are heedless of the very prayer they are performing. They do not perform it properly. What Allah desires is that prayer be established correctly; mere performance is not what is required, and prayer is established only when it is recited with its religious spirit and its meanings, and in which the presence of Allah's Being is kept in mind.

For this reason, the prayer that they are performing does not produce its effects in their lives, because they are heedless during the movements of prayer. Accordingly, these people do not even give the small necessity (ma'un) to others. They do not perform any assistance, kindness or goodness to others, whereas the demand of prayer is that the worshipper does good to Allah's servants and does not withhold small necessities from them. Therefore those of this kind are in fact not performing true prayer. Hence, the standard of true and genuine worship before Allah is that a person does not withhold small necessities from humanity, and does not withdraw from helping them.

Thus we find ourselves confronted with another inseparable truth of the religion, and it is the demand of the Islamic worldview: a Qur'anic verse openly threatens worshippers that they will face destruction, because they are not establishing prayer properly. Rather, they are performing movements that have no spirit in them. They are not present in the court of Allah during these movements. They are not sincerely for Allah; rather, they pray merely to be seen by people, so the effects that true prayer produces do not appear from their prayer, neither does prayer affect their hearts, nor does it influence their practical world. Therefore this prayer is worthless as a particle, a mere dust, and for the worshipper it is rather a calamity and destruction.

After these explanations, it becomes clearly understood why Allah sends messengers to people and why it is demanded of people that they believe and serve. This entire striving brings no benefit to Allah; He is the Self-Sufficient King. The purpose is that human lives themselves be made good, their welfare is intended, their hearts be purified and their lives be successful. He desires for them a life founded upon pure consciousness and lofty ideals, within which people are sponsors of one another, whose mentality is noble, within which there is love and brotherhood, and whose outlook and conduct are both pure.

Alas! Where is humanity heading, having abandoned this goodness? Where is it wandering, having abandoned this mercy? And into what depths has it fallen, having abandoned this beautiful, graceful and lofty station? Or where is it lost in the intricate and dark paths of ignorance (jahiliyyah), while before it the light, the light of Islam, stands present at the central crossroads.
